newsitem.title: JAPAN: New ANA chief hopes to steer clear of turbulence.
newsitem.headline: New ANA chief hopes to steer clear of turbulence.

text.p: The next president of Japan's All Nippon Airways Co Ltd, buffeted by a series of management wrangles, said on Thursday that he is determined to steer the troubled airline into clearer skies.
"I will do my very best to reunite the company. What we need to do now is to regain public trust and boost sales," Kichisaburo Nomura, ANA's president-designate, told reporters.

Japan's top domestic carrier, reeling from a chain of resignations by top officials in the last two weeks, had previously named Kenzo Yoshikawa as its incoming president but, in a sudden change of direction, announced on Thursday that Nomura would take the post instead.
Also on Thursday, ANA chairman Takaya Sugiura said he was resigning from the chairmanship and his post as a director in June in order to "calm down the confusion" in the company.
About one-third of the board of directors will also step down and be replaced by new members in late June, ANA said.

The sweeping management reshuffle started with the company's abrupt announcement on May 13 that Yoshikawa, currently the president of related firm ANA Real Estate Co Ltd, would replace the current president, Seiji Fukatsu.

Fukatsu was said to have decided to quit after disagreements with chairman Sugiura and honorary chairman Tokuji Wakasa, an 82-year-old former vice transport minister, over cost-cutting policies and personnel issues.
The incident ignited criticism from many ANA employees who oppose a management structure controlled by former government officials, Japanese media reports said.
Last week, Wakasa announced he would resign as a director.

President-designate Nomura, who is currently a senior managing director and will assume the presidency in late June, told reporters: "I would like to continue putting president Fukatsu's management policies into effect in order to overcome this difficult situation in Japan's airline industry."
Tensions from the personnel drama have put an extra burden on ANA, already struggling with high fuel costs and increasing competition.

The carrier announced on Thursday that for the current 1997/98 business year which started on April 1, it expected to post a parent current profit only slightly larger than its actual profit in 1996/97.

ANA said it sees a parent current profit of 17.5 billion yen ($150 million) in 1997/98, up one percent from its actual 1996/97 parent current profit. Current profit is pre-tax and includes gains and losses from investments.

For the year ended March 31, it posted a parent current profit of 17.33 billion yen ($149 million), up 2.9 percent from the previous year. Sales rose 4.9 percent from the previous year to 887.41 billion yen ($7.65 billion), ANA said.
A rise in fuel prices and growing domestic price competition posed challenges for the company's management in the last business year, ANA said in a statement.
"ANA will continue with internal reform and cost-cutting to increase competitiveness," the statement said. ($1=116 yen)
